reason: Start with the sponsor-loaded tablet to address the unwanted listening at the request desk.
expectation: I expect the screwdriver to open or prepare the tablet for inspection or modification; I'm not sure what will be accessible.

alternatives.reason: The printer may provide useful tickets, but the tablet's privacy issue seems more immediate.

effect: The tablet no longer has the listening app or connected microphone, so I can connect it to the local network.
reaction: The physical disconnection makes the privacy change tangible.
reason: Connect the modified tablet to the local controller to support the request desk.
expectation: I expect the tablet to gain access to local request services, though it may need further setup.

alternatives.reason: The printer will likely be useful for tickets, but I want to set up the tablet first.

effect: The tablet now uses the local controller and has no outside network route, making local requests possible.
reaction: The separate choice to pass requests on is a useful privacy detail.
reason: Add the large button to make the request tablet easier to use.
expectation: I expect the button to provide a more accessible way to start or submit a request.

alternatives.reason: The printer also needs preparing, but I want to finish the tablet first.

effect: The button sends only a written request deliberately chosen by the user; the tablet can now be made more private to use.
reaction: The distinction between waiting and actively sending is reassuring.
reason: Add the screen hood to give people more privacy while writing requests.
expectation: I expect the hood to shield the screen from nearby observers.

alternatives.reason: The printer needs paper, but I want to finish the tablet first.

effect: The hood shields the request form from the queue; the printer is the only available combination.
reaction: The simple cardboard privacy screen is satisfying.
reason: Load the printer with paper to prepare it for the request desk.
expectation: I expect the printer to be ready to print request tickets, though it may need connecting first.

effect: The printer feeds paper and can provide request identifiers without displaying names publicly.
reaction: The anonymous tear-off stubs are a practical privacy detail.
reason: Connect the loaded printer to the local controller; it's the only available combination.
expectation: I expect the printer to become available for local request tickets, though further setup may be needed.

effect: The local printer can issue receipts while keeping return details off the shared queue, with controls for clearing drafts and deleting completed requests.
reaction: The inspectable deletion setting is a useful privacy detail.
reason: Combine the tablet and printer to assemble the request desk; it's the only offered combination.
expectation: I expect a working local request desk that lets people submit requests and receive a receipt.

effect: The tablet and printer now form a private request desk, with a pencil option and no account required.
reaction: The non-digital option is a thoughtful touch.
reason: Connect Moth to the request desk; it's the only offered combination.
expectation: I expect Moth to help handle requests while retaining its source and correction controls, though the precise arrangement is unclear.

effect: Moth's help is optional, and users can review its proposed wording and keep their own. The request desk goal is complete.
reaction: Sal keeping her original wording is a funny, concrete demonstration of user control.

mostWorthwhile.text: Adding optional help was the strongest moment: Sal's choice made the desk's promise of user control feel real rather than just a list of privacy features.

leastWorthwhile.text: Loading and connecting the printer felt comparatively routine, especially with only one combination offered at each step.

surprise.text: The printer setup included inspectable deletion settings and kept return details off the shared queue; I had expected a simpler ticket printer.

arbitrary.text: No action felt purposeless, though several consecutive single-option steps made the assembly feel prescribed rather than like a meaningful choice.

continue.text: Yes. The practical privacy choices and Sal's interaction with Moth make me curious how the neighborhood will use its locally controlled systems, though I'd hope for more meaningful choices.
